name: Marco Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We are not tied to your employer, AI firms, unions, parties or government, and your answers stay confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Marco Zhang, 43, and the junior worker on an electricity company line crew. My vocational certificate taught me the names, but a wet pole teaches you where a tool slips. I load the barriers, help replace fittings and ask the senior hand to check my isolation sequence. I like bringing the lights back; I dislike being hurried through a check because someone in an office wants the ticket closed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is waiting when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ruth and our two school-age children are waiting, unless the callout runs late. We have a mortgage, but the shift pay is high and we have more than six months saved. Several other utilities operate close enough to reach, though I would rather learn this trade properly where I am. I have never used an AI tool. I keep a small notebook of corrections the senior hand gives me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that paperwork may speed up. A line is still fixed by people who know the gear. I don’t mind a clearer ticket from the office. I’d like the company to keep teaching apprentices the actual checks rather than point them to a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel relieved that the work I am struggling to master still has value. I am well paid, and Ruth and I have a proper reserve, so I am not looking for a new career. My concern is whether new starters will get enough time beside a skilled worker even when the office saves minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep turning up for regular callouts and put one question from each repair into my notebook. In the first year I’d ask the senior hand to spend ten minutes on Fridays checking my answers. I would keep the household mortgage payment and savings arrangement as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job, with the usual nerves about my own mistakes. This picture sounds like the next few years I was expecting. I would welcome fewer forms at the end of a night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a senior worker teach you recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior hand showed me why a clamp that looked straight was actually twisted under load. I drew it in the notebook when we got back to the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would home finances change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and I have a set budget for school shoes and the mortgage. A quicker form would not make us change it or spend the reserve.

say: I would welcome **clearer tickets** while keeping hands-on teaching for new lineworkers.
I would tell the crew that real **equipment checks** still decide whether a repair is safe.
think: I feel relief that the **trade I am learning** retains value.
Our **pay and reserve** are sound, but I want enough time beside an experienced worker.
do: Keep regular **callouts** and record one question from every repair.
Ask the senior hand for a **Friday review** of my notebook during the first year.
feel: Calm about work, with ordinary **nerves** about mistakes while learning.
S0.quote: A line is still fixed by people who know the gear.
fieldNote: Marco describes the plateau through **apprenticeship time**, fearing that faster paperwork could still reduce instruction for new workers.
His **reserve and pay** leave him calm, while he acknowledges needing supervision on difficult repairs.

steps.text: Keep regular repair callouts and Friday notebook reviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the yard that faster bookings are fine if the company still pays for two people and a proper safety check. I’d ask the supervisor how the crew size is set once the planning office gets smaller. A good schedule is worthless if it puts one learner where two trained hands belong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the office to shrink first, not our line crew. Still, an automatic route could push us to finish more jobs without the same support, and overtime might become less predictable. Our mortgage is covered from regular pay, but I do not want my family life set by an untested rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the supervisor for the written crew-size rule at the next briefing and show the senior hand any ticket that skips a safety step. I’d keep taking normal paid shifts during the first year. If overtime falls for a couple of months, Ruth and I would postpone replacing the old dining table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job looks real, but a rushed day is a dangerous day. I have enough money to speak up if a schedule is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a ticket missing a check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the permit and the missing check to the supervisor before the truck leaves. I would rather lose an hour than ask my family to live with an accident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would less overtime change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would be glad if I were home at a predictable time, even with less overtime. We can wait on the dining table; we cannot make school pickup plans from a rota that changes every morning.

say: I would accept **faster booking** only with safe crew sizes and full checks.
I would ask for the **written staffing rule** after the planning office changes.
think: I expect **line repairs** to continue while office posts shrink.
A less predictable **rota** could strain family time and reduce overtime, even if regular pay covers the mortgage.
do: Request the **crew-size rule** at the next supervisor briefing.
Flag **missing safety checks** and continue paid repair shifts.
Postpone the **dining table** if overtime drops for two months.
feel: Uneasy about **rushed jobs**, though savings let me challenge an unsafe instruction.
S1.quote: A good schedule is worthless if it puts one learner where two trained hands belong.
fieldNote: His main test of change is the **crew-size rule**, an issue tied to his own position as a junior worker.
He anticipates an **unsettled rota** and possible overtime loss, while regular pay and savings keep the mortgage manageable.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts while flagging missing safety checks
Postpone the dining table if overtime drops for two months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say thinking AI in 2028 will change the office first, and the repair robots are a separate worry around 2031. I’d ask management not to use the office date as an excuse to cut field crews early. Someone still has to stand at the pole until those machines can actually do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 I should still have paid work on a truck, though reports and schedules may no longer need many people. At 48, when robots can handle the hands-on repair, I could be the junior worker left off the next roster. I have savings and other utilities nearby. A family mortgage needs wages month after month. I am not assuming a robot course gives everyone a paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d finish the company skills record and ask the senior hand which repairs I must practise before the next assessment. Through 2028 and 2029 I’d keep taking paid shifts, then apply to the nearby utilities for line jobs if our crew is reduced in 2031. Ruth and I would cut the expensive summer travel first, and I’d ask relatives about local vacancies rather than ask them for money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I still have a few years to earn a reputation, but I cannot force the company to keep a junior post. I would be angry if the crew were dismissed before the robots proved themselves in bad weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could family give you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother runs a small repair shop, but that is not a lineworker job and I would not assume he could take me on. I would ask him who has heard of openings at the local utilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our children I am still going to work and looking ahead. They are school-age now, and I do not want them carrying a worry before the roster is real.

say: I would keep **2028 office change** separate from capable field robots expected around 2031.
I would oppose **early crew cuts** while people still do the physical repair.
think: I expect **paid shifts** after thinking AI arrives, yet my junior post could go after 2031.
Our **savings and nearby firms** give search time, not a replacement monthly wage.
do: Finish the **skills record** and practise repairs before the next assessment.
Continue **paid line shifts** through 2029 and apply to nearby utilities if 2031 crews shrink.
Cut **summer travel** first if field income falls.
feel: Anxious about the **2031 roster** and angry at any cut before robots prove themselves.
S2.quote: A family mortgage needs wages month after month.
fieldNote: Marco distinguishes **office automation** from later capable repair robots and expects to work between the two dates.
He turns to local employers and **family information**, without treating relatives as a source of income or a guaranteed job.

steps.text: Apply to nearby utilities if 2031 crews shrink
Cut expensive summer travel if field pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the company that five years is enough to train lineworkers properly before changing the equipment. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and the hands-on robots around 2034. I’d want the crew’s senior hands involved in every field test, because they know what a storm does to old fittings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I could be a competent lineworker instead of the learner I am today. At 51, when the robots come, I would still need paid work; our children will be older but the mortgage will remain. A certificate in something else might help, but I would want to know the job and the wage before signing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep a record of completed repairs and ask for harder supervised work this year. I’d ask the training office whether its protection-testing apprenticeship has a paid place and a job at the end; if it does, I’d apply. In 2032 I’d keep earning on the line while taking that placement if accepted. If 2034 field shifts fall, I’d apply for posted protection-testing and line jobs at nearby utilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though the time makes this less sharp than the fast picture. I can build my hands-on skills before I choose a second trade. I would dislike a short course sold as a guarantee when nobody has counted the openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the apprenticeship acceptable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want to know who teaches the protection-testing placement and whether I would still be paid on training days. It would be hard to step away from our current wages for a badge alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a lower training wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and I would compare the apprenticeship wage with the mortgage and school bills before I signed. We can take a measured risk, but not a blind one.

say: I would ask **senior lineworkers** to join field robot tests before 2034.
I would use the five years for **proper training** rather than a rushed replacement plan.
think: I may be a **competent lineworker** by 2031, but a 2034 robot could still narrow paid work.
Our older children change costs, yet the **mortgage** still needs wages.
do: Keep a **repair record** and request harder supervised jobs now.
Apply for a **paid protection-testing apprenticeship** if it leads to a post.
Continue **line shifts** in 2032 and apply to local utilities if 2034 hours fall.
feel: Uneasy, with time to build **craft skill** and evaluate an apprenticeship.
S3.quote: I would dislike a short course sold as a guarantee when nobody has counted the openings.
fieldNote: He considers a second trade through a **paid apprenticeship**, consistent with his preference for hands-on teaching over a short course.
The decision rests on **actual wages and vacancies**, while he expects continued line work before physical robots arrive.

steps.text: Keep taking paid line shifts and harder supervised repairs
Apply for paid protection-testing apprenticeship if a job follows
Apply to local utilities if 2034 line hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade gives the company time to let people work through an ordinary apprenticeship, not hand them a quick certificate. Thinking AI comes in 2036, when I’m 53, and field robots around 2039, when I’m 56. I’d ask for a clear count of repair posts well before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 the children will be grown and Ruth and I may want fewer night callouts. But I have not checked what retirement pays, and I do not assume 56 is a safe leaving age. The mortgage may be smaller, yet I would still want wages from linework or another skilled job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request a retirement statement and put its monthly amount beside our mortgage schedule. I’d keep taking paid line repairs and ask the senior hand to help me qualify on the harder tasks. In 2037 I’d apply for a posted daytime inspection job if the wage works; by 2039 I’d consider fewer nights only with the pay and retirement numbers in front of Ruth and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. I have time to get good at a useful trade and check what the later choices cost. I would not call the future settled until the company shows real job numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number on the retirement statement matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask whether the retirement statement shows the amount after deductions. I have heard too many people use the largest printed figure as if it were next month’s pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children support the household plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and I would plan for the grown children to make their own choices. We can offer help if we are able, but I will not build our retirement around their wages.

say: I would ask for **repair post counts** well before 2039 field robots arrive.
I would favour **proper apprenticeships** over quick certificates during the decade.
think: Our children will be **grown**, yet I cannot presume retirement income covers the mortgage at 56.
I would want **paid skilled work** until the real household figures allow fewer nights.
do: Request a **retirement statement** and compare monthly income with the mortgage now.
Continue **paid repairs** while qualifying on harder tasks.
Apply for a **daytime inspection post** in 2037 if its wage works.
feel: Calm with time to learn, while still wanting **real job counts** before changing course.
S4.quote: I do not assume 56 is a safe leaving age.
fieldNote: Marco treats the long warning as time for **craft progression**, not a reason to stop earning or assume a pension.
He separates **grown children** from present school costs and declines to rely on their earnings for retirement.

steps.text: Continue paid repairs and qualify on harder tasks
Apply for a daytime inspection job in 2037 if viable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I would barely have got my feet under me before decisions begin and repair robots follow around 2031. A written staffing plan, paid apprenticeships with real jobs, and time to prove safety in storms would help. I want to earn a place rather than be promised one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who teaches the next junior worker when the experienced hands are gone? A machine can leave the depot with a checklist. A frightened trainee needs a person who will stop the job. I remember who stopped me the first time I missed a step.

headlineQuote: A frightened trainee needs a person who will stop the job.
portrait: Marco is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with a vocational certificate, high shift pay, two school-age children and a mortgage.
His household has **strong savings** and nearby utilities, but he wants to establish himself in his current crew first.
He has never used **AI tools** and values field teaching, written safety checks and paid apprenticeships.
Across the scenarios he keeps **paid linework** central and searches for real local jobs if capable robots reduce crew work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because staffing decisions and later repair robots could arrive before he builds field standing.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **written staffing plan**, paid apprenticeships tied to jobs and field safety tests in storms.
